summary: Link-local IPv6 addresses need a zone identifier (such as an interface name) to say which network link they belong to. This document explains how users should type that identifier into user interfaces such as address fields. It replaces RFC 6874 and updates RFC 4007, RFC 7622 and RFC 8089.

plainLanguage.summary: Some IPv6 addresses only make sense on one particular network cable or wireless link, so they need an extra label saying which one. This document says that any program that asks you to type such an address must also let you give that label, so people can type the whole address in one go.

subtitle: How a program that asks for an IPv6 address should also let the user say which link it is on.

tldr.problem: A link-local IPv6 address such as fe80::1 is only meaningful on one network link, so a program that asks the user to type such an address also has to know which interface it belongs to. Many user interfaces have no way to collect that, which forces people to work around it.
tldr.mechanism: The document requires any user interface that accepts a non-global IPv6 address to provide a way to enter a link-local or scoped multicast address together with a zone identifier, and to support the standard percent-sign form such as fe80::1%eth0.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9844 replaces RFC 6874, which browser implementers found impracticable to support, and replaces it with a requirement aimed at user interfaces rather than at the URI syntax. It also updates RFC 4007, RFC 7622 and RFC 8089.

today: RFC 9844 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It replaced RFC 6874 and updates RFC 4007, RFC 7622 and RFC 8089, so it is the current statement of how user interfaces should handle IPv6 zone identifiers.

sections.title: What a Zone Identifier Is
sections.content:
A number of software tools require or permit the user to enter an IPv6 address via a user interface. The standard literal text format for an IPv6 address is defined by RFC 4291 and RFC 5952. The IPv6 Scoped Address Architecture specification, RFC 4007, extends the text representation of limited-scope IPv6 addresses, in particular link-local unicast addresses and multicast addresses with less than global scope, so that a zone identifier may be concatenated to an address.

Zone identifiers are especially useful where literal addresses are typically used, for example during fault diagnosis or device configuration, when it may be essential to specify which interface is used for sending to a link-local address. A zone identifier has purely local meaning within the node in which it is defined, and is usually the same as an IPv6 interface name. It is completely meaningless for any other node. At the time of writing it is meaningful only when attached to link-local unicast and scoped multicast addresses, but other uses might be defined in the future.

Examples of a link-local unicast address qualified by a zone identifier are fe80::1234%eth0 on a Linux host and fe80::4321%7 on a Microsoft Windows host. Such addresses are directly supported by socket API calls including getaddrinfo(). Devices whose network stack does not support the human-readable zone identifier described in RFC 4007 are out of scope for this document.
sections.plainLanguage: A link-local address is like a street address that only makes sense inside one building. The zone identifier says which building. On a Linux computer it is usually the interface name, such as eth0, and on Windows it is often a number, such as 7.

sections.title: Where Zone Identifiers Are Needed
sections.content:
The document gives five examples of use cases for entering an address that includes a zone identifier. A debugging tool may check whether an interface works and whether a device exists by running ping fe80::1234%eth0; if it succeeds, the user learns that the other device is reachable via the interface named eth0. A tool may have to configure or reconfigure a device that only has a link-local address, for example a home router that is reachable at 192.168.178.1 but not at fe80::1%eth0, and link-local addresses need to be entered in network management user interfaces for formats such as YANG.

A monitoring tool such as a network sniffer may need to specify a given link-local address on a given interface whose traffic is of interest. The Microsoft Web Services for Devices virtual printer port mechanism can present the user with an IPv6 link-local address such as fe80::823b:f9ff:fe7b:d9dc%10 in which the zone identifier is present but is not recognized by appropriate software. The National Marine Electronics Association has defined the OneNet Marine IPv6 Ethernet Networking Standard, which uses IPv6 link-local addresses exclusively, and proposed improvements include a web page for device configuration using link-local addresses.

For all such use cases it is highly desirable that a complete IPv6 link-local address can be cut and pasted from one user interface to another. Since such addresses may include quite long hexadecimal strings, for example fe80::8d0f:7f26:f5c8:780b%enx525400d5e0fb, any solution except cut-and-paste is highly error prone.
sections.plainLanguage: People need this when they are diagnosing a network, configuring a device that has no other address, or filtering captured traffic. Because these addresses are long and easy to mistype, being able to copy one from a terminal window into a configuration form matters.

sections.title: Relationship to Other Documents
sections.content:
The zone identifiers that can be used are limited by the host operating system, since RFC 4007 only specifies that they are text strings, without specifying a maximum length or syntax. Each zone identifier corresponds to a numerical zone index that qualifies a link-local address. Although some operating systems and network APIs support a default zone identifier as recommended by RFC 4007, others, including Linux, do not, and for them a solution is particularly important, since a link-local address without a zone index cannot be used in the Linux socket API.

The model in RFC 4007 assumes that the human-readable zone identifier is mapped by the operating system into a numeric interface index, typically by the socket API through getaddrinfo(). The mapping between the human-readable string and the numeric value is a host-specific function that varies between operating systems. This document is concerned only with the human-readable string that is typically displayed in an operating system's user interface. In most operating systems it is possible to use the underlying interface number, represented as a decimal integer, as an equivalent to the human-readable string, which is recommended by Section 11.2 of RFC 4007 but is not required.

This document completely obsoletes RFC 6874, which implementors of web browsers have determined is impracticable to support, and replaces it with a generic user interface requirement. Obsoleting RFC 6874 reverts the change it made to the URI syntax defined by RFC 3986, so RFC 3986 is no longer updated by RFC 6874. The document also updates RFC 7622 and RFC 8089 by deleting their references to RFC 6874, and updates RFC 4007 by adding a new requirement that user interfaces support the zone identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: The older document on this topic, RFC 6874, tried to change how web addresses are written, and browser makers decided that was not workable. This document drops that approach and simply asks programs to offer a way to enter the zone identifier.

sections.title: What the Interface Must Offer
sections.content:
A user interface that allows or requires the user to enter an IPv6 address other than a global unicast address MUST provide a means for entering a link-local address or a scoped multicast address and selecting a zone identifier as specified by RFC 4007, typically an interface identifier as defined by the operating system. In that case the user interface SHOULD support the complete format specified by RFC 4007, for example fe80::1%eth0.

If that is impossible for practical reasons, the user interface MAY support an alternative delimiter in place of the percent sign. The hyphen is suggested, for example fe80::1-eth0. If that too is impossible for practical reasons, the user interface MAY provide two separate input fields, for example fe80::1 in one box and eth0 in another, selection from a list of active zone identifiers, or a separate command-line parameter for the zone identifier.

Because this model treats the zone identifier as independent of the IPv6 address, it does not resolve the difficulties in considering the zone identifier as part of the HTTP origin model. The approach therefore does not resolve the issue of how browsers should support link-local addresses, and the recommendations and normative statements in this document do not apply to URIs fetched by web browsers.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule is that the form has to work: a program that asks for an IPv6 address must accept one with a zone on it. The preferred spelling puts the zone after a percent sign, but a different separator or a separate box for the zone is acceptable if the percent sign is impractical.

sections.title: Turning the Zone Name into an Index
sections.content:
The program providing the user interface stores the address and the zone identifier, converting the latter to an interface index, typically via the socket API. A faulty zone identifier is detected when attempting to convert it, and this should be reported to the user as an error. The resulting interface index is used for any subsequent socket calls using the link-local address.

An address string such as fe80::1%eth0 cannot be converted to binary by the POSIX socket API function inet_pton(). It must be converted either by using getaddrinfo(), or by splitting it into two strings and using inet_pton() and if_nametoindex() successively, in order to obtain the required interface index value.
sections.plainLanguage: What the user types is turned into a number that identifies the network interface, and that number is what the operating system actually uses. If the name does not match an interface, the program should say so rather than carrying on.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Zone identifiers are of local significance only and must not be sent on the wire. Software should not trust packets that contain textual non-global addresses as data. Software that obtains a zone identifier through a user interface should therefore not transmit it further.

There is no formal limit on the length of the zone identifier string in RFC 4007. A user interface implementation should apply an appropriate length limit when inputting a zone identifier, in order to minimize the risk of a buffer overrun. Typically this limit would be the same as the host operating system's limit on interface names.

RFC 4007 does not specify or restrict the character set allowed in a zone identifier, so each implementation processing zone identifiers needs to make checks appropriate for the environment it is used in. For example, a user interface implementation should not allow ASCII NUL characters in a zone identifier string, as this could cause inconsistencies in subsequent string processing.
sections.plainLanguage: The zone name is only meaningful on the machine where it was typed, so it should never be sent over the network. The program should also limit how long the name can be and should reject odd characters such as embedded nulls.

items.title: The full format
items.text: The complete address with a percent sign, such as fe80::1%eth0. This is what the document prefers.

items.title: Another delimiter
items.text: A hyphen is suggested, giving fe80::1-eth0, if the percent sign is impractical.

items.title: A separate field
items.text: Two boxes, one for the address and one for the zone, or a list of active zones, or a separate command-line parameter.
